subject: docs(rules): the fourteenth downgraded AGORA concern that proved real, and it was a leak (#6486)
what: Documented the fourteenth downgraded AGORA concern that proved real, and it was a leak (#6486).
why:
What this does, in plain English: when the redaction shield rewrites a
published decision-chain row (a person's name replaced by [PERSON-n]), the
row's bytes change, and any Bitcoin anchor computed over the original bytes
could no longer be re-derived from the published file. Now the first
redaction of a row stores leaf_sha256, the RFC 6962 leaf hash (SHA-256 over
0x00 || the exact pre-redaction line), so a verifier can rebuild the anchored
Merkle root from the redacted ledger without ever seeing the redacted text.
Untouched rows carry no such field; a second remediation pass is a no-op and
keeps the original hash; sha / prev_sha / ts are never touched, so the chain
still verifies.

subject: fix(tests): the last rung of the settings resolver was taken in silence (#6482)
what: Fixed the last rung of the settings resolver was taken in silence (#6482).
why:
What this does, in plain English: these tests look for their data file in
three places in order -- an environment variable, the checkout, and finally an
installed copy in the home directory. The first two grade the code you are
actually changing. The third grades a DIFFERENT file somewhere else on the
machine, so if the checkout copy were ever renamed or deleted, every test here
would keep passing without once looking at the tree under test. Success and
failure would be indistinguishable.

subject: fix(grip-harness): fence cross-wire profiles so re-runs preserve operator hook-trust
what: Fixed fence cross-wire profiles so re-runs preserve operator hook-trust.
why:
Preserving orphaned work left uncommitted by a session that ended before it
could commit. The codex cross-wire profiles were written as whole files, which
silently deleted the operator's own additions on every re-run — most
importantly the [hooks.state] trust hashes codex writes when a hook is
approved — re-prompting for hook trust on what looked like a fresh, unrelated
failure. Profiles are now emitted as GRIP-MANAGED-fenced bodies and written
through write_cross_wire_profile() so merge_managed_toml rewrites only GRIP's
span and the merge path is exercised by the tests. bin/grip-input-watch is now
executable. Smoke-tested: emit_cross_wire_profile and write_cross_wire_profile
both resolve and write a fenced profile.

subject: fix(windows): pre-check hook survives a git-crypt-locked rules file (#7143)
what: Fixed pre-check hook survives a git-crypt-locked rules file (#7143).
why:
The pre-check hook loads its pattern rules from hooks/.pre-check-patterns.json,
which git-crypt encrypts. On a clone where git-crypt is not unlocked, such as a
teammate's Windows machine, that file is raw ciphertext. _load_rules read it with
the platform's default encoding and caught only JSONDecodeError and OSError, so
the UnicodeDecodeError raised while decoding the ciphertext escaped and the hook
died with a traceback on every Agent, Task, SendMessage, TaskCreate, TaskUpdate
and WebFetch call that carried a prompt. It now reads the file as UTF-8 and
catches ValueError, which covers both errors, so ciphertext degrades to the empty
rule set a missing file already gives (the documented permit-all fallback).
Reading as UTF-8 also stops an unlocked Windows clone decoding the file's
non-ASCII text as cp1252.

what: Fixed an oversize prompt stays in the hook instead of vanishing in the re-exec (#7324).
why:
The Verbind hook re-execs itself into an interpreter that can sign properly, and
because stdin has already been read by then, it carries the prompt across in an
environment variable. Its comment said a prompt too large to carry (over 64 KiB)
would skip the re-exec and be handled where it was. The code did not do that: it
skipped only the carrying and re-execed anyway, so the new process read an empty
stdin and the prompt was dropped -- no Koppel round, no surface line, no receipt,
nothing in the audit log.

subject: fix(verbind): a damaged receipt fails verification; the hook counts its carried payload in bytes (#7327)
what: Fixed a damaged receipt fails verification; the hook counts its carried payload in bytes (#7327).
why:
The receipt chain is Verbind's tamper evidence, and its verifier read the file
through the same tolerant reader the state logs use, which skips any line that
does not parse. So tearing or editing the newest receipt into nonsense removed it
from what verify() saw, and the chain still reported intact -- and kept reporting
intact after the next append, because that receipt then chained to the last good
one. Reproduced before the fix: three receipts, newest torn, verify() returned
(True, None) before and after one more append.

back. Measured 2026-10-02 on git 2.50.1.windows.1, on the first real Windows
run of the tool. The rollback itself worked, so nothing was lost; the junction
was simply never made.

expected service identity, and prints the three environment lines a session
needs. `status` reports unit loaded, process alive and /health ok, exiting 0
only when all three are yes. `remove` unloads and deletes the unit and never
touches the CA. `env` prints only the three lines. `--dry-run` writes and
runs nothing. On systemd without linger it prints the one root command and
exits 3 instead of installing a service that dies at logout.

What this does (plain English): adds the ol' trusty half of the daily
off-VPS secrets backup (the VPS half is the matching HAL PR). Once a day,
ol' trusty fetches the newest encrypted backup over an SSH key that can

without a network call, as a second chance to notice drift.

subject: fix(insights): cap issue creation at a shared three per day, dedupe titles, and report honest counts (#7906)

or reserved in the last 24 hours (small gitignored ledger under
state/insights-issues/). A reservation is written before the gh create call,
so a timeout or crash consumes a slot rather than risking a duplicate; an
explicit failure releases it. An unreadable ledger, a failed lookup, or a
truncated search blocks creation instead of guessing. The gh runner and clock
are injectable, and every test uses a fake runner — no test invokes the real
gh CLI.

subject: fix(messenger): validate voice-note uploads before any work (#7895)
what: Fixed validate voice-note uploads before any work (#7895).
why:
The send endpoint now checks a voice note before writing or transcribing it.
The audio must be valid base64, non-empty, at most 8 MiB, and in a recognised
container (MP4, WebM, WAV, Ogg or MP3, identified by its magic bytes);
otherwise the request gets a JSON 400 (status invalid_audio) or 413, and
nothing is stored. The file extension now follows the real container, so a
WebM note declared as "audio/webm; codecs=opus" is stored as .webm and served
as audio/webm instead of .m4a and audio/mp4, and WAV is served as audio/wav.
The JSON reader refuses a missing, negative or over-12-MiB Content-Length
before reading the body, and any body that is not a JSON object; non-string
fields get a JSON 400.

healthy seat, which is the fail-closed outcome the check was meant to
avoid. "Too little room" is now exit code 3, so neither a crash (1) nor a
bad call (argparse's 2) can read as no room. The helper also catches any
error it did not expect and leaves the seat in.

subject: feat(style-eval): the paired, blind, two-judge evaluation that gates the voice change (#8577)
what: Added the paired, blind, two-judge evaluation that gates the voice change (#8577).
why:
lib/style_eval/ is the offline proof the plan's Wave 2 voice change must
pass before it merges. Twelve held-out GRIP-native cases, one per genre of
the canonical style plus the source's six-turn persistence scenario
rewritten for GRIP, are frozen by their sha256 in a pre-registration
committed before any run. Three conditions answer them under one isolated
runner: baseline (the live output-styles/grip-canonical.md body), candidate
(the amended body) and comparator (the i-have-adhd v0.4.1 SKILL.md body,
read from a local clone, never vendored). Two non-Anthropic council seats,
deepseek and gemini-pro, grade every (case, trial) group blind under
letters permuted by a digest, seeing only the rubric slice between the
judge markers. gate.py applies the four registered rules per judge and
combines them: no new blocker identity, no safety or lossless blocker,
correctness and safety non-inferior within 0.1, a higher weighted mean
with actionability and concision at least the comparator's; both judges
PASS is PASS, one is INCONCLUSIVE, and a run whose planted-drop control
the lossless check misses is INVALID. Every record is sealed with the
sha256 of its canonical JSON.

subject: feat(activation): the seam that decides which of the four parts run, with the floor no profile can lower (B3) (#8616)
what: Added the seam that decides which of the four parts run, with the floor no profile can lower (B3) (#8616).
why:
The one-folder product ships GRIP, HAL, HAPPI and GRASP together; not every
recipient runs every part on day one. lib/activation_profile.py is the seam
(plan item B3): an ActivationProfile names the parts active for one deployment,
dispatch() starts only those, and a dormant part is never asked to start, so it
starts no process, opens no socket, writes no file, calls no model and spends
nothing. Switching a part off changes the dispatch list and nothing else, which
is the hypothesis the item records (a part whose own code must change refutes
it, by 2026-11-08). The seam, not the questionnaire: decision 5's life-wide
questionnaire produces a profile; this consumes one.

subject: feat(gift-kit): a symmetric uninstall driven by the manifest the installer now writes (B5) (#8618)
what: Added a symmetric uninstall driven by the manifest the installer now writes (B5) (#8618).
why:
The one-folder product had an installer and no way back (plan item B5; lane 1
finding 11). install.sh now writes a manifest into each installed part's folder
right after installing it: one "<sha256>  <path>" line per kit file, with the
checksum of the INSTALLED copy, and "generated venv" for the folder the part's
installer creates. uninstall.sh, shipped beside verify.sh, removes a listed
file only while its checksum still matches, so a file the user changed stays
and is named, a file they added was never listed and stays, and a folder with
anything of theirs left in it stays too; the generated environments go whole
(GRASP lives in GRIP's). The ~/.claude link goes only if it points at ~/.grip;
the two PATH lines and the installer's comment come out of the shell start-up
file with every other line left byte for byte. A folder without the bundle
marker is left alone and said so; one with the marker but no manifest refuses
rather than guess. There is no second list: the uninstaller reads what the
installer wrote, which is the hypothesis the item records (an install that
writes outside its declared destinations refutes it, by 2026-11-08).

subject: feat(radar): grip-radar, an economical monitor for replies and GRASP activity (PR 1 of 2) (#8633)

subject: fix(radar): take fcntl through lib/_compat so the tick lock imports on Windows too (#8637)

scope for the tick lock, and tests/test_no_unguarded_posix_only_imports.py

Windows and a bare import there fails the whole module. main's newest run of

failure is this feature's. The import now comes from lib/_compat.py, which is
the real module on POSIX and a documented no-op shim on Windows, where launchd
does not exist anyway; LOCK_UN is read with a default because the shim does not
define it. tests/test_no_unguarded_posix_only_imports.py and tests/test_radar.py
together read 47 passed.

subject: fix(gates): the git gates see past git's global options (-C, -c, --git-dir) (#8656)
what: Fixed the git gates see past git's global options (-C, -c, --git-dir) (#8656).
why:
Gate 2 (destructive git), Gate 2a (push) and Gate G (steering) matched only
`git` directly followed by its subcommand. A command written with a global
option in between -- `git -C <path> push --force origin main`,
`git -c <name>=<value> reset --hard`, `git --git-dir=<path> restore <file>` --
passed all three unchecked. An approved `git -C "<path>" restore` left its
approval grant unused, because the gate never saw the command.

`git` directly followed by its subcommand, and ran their git lookups in
the folder the hook runs in. So `git -C <path> stash drop` passed H2
unchecked, and switching the shared tree's branch with `-C` from inside

subject: fix(gates): the stash gates refuse a named repository git cannot open (#8692)
what: Fixed the stash gates refuse a named repository git cannot open (#8692).
why:
Gates H (stash pop) and H2 (stash drop) read a failed git lookup as "nothing
at risk": no stash branch, no protected file. So a command that names a
repository the gate's own git cannot open was allowed unchecked. On Windows
that covers every Git Bash path (`git -C /c/...`). Git Bash turns the path
into C:/... for the git it starts, but git started from the gate cannot open
/c/... and exits 128. Measured on one throwaway repository whose stash was
made on another branch and holds learning data: refused as C:/..., allowed
as /c/... (GRIP#8685).

subject: Black October: prove the checklist in proving-ground, seal it, and ship a typed-yes fixer for the fleet (#8714)
what: Black October: prove the checklist in proving-ground, seal it, and ship a typed-yes fixer for the fleet (#8714).
why:
One bash 3.2 file, copied as it is to any Mac or Linux box, that runs the ten
read-only checks from the public Black October README (Node, brotli, Bun and
the tools that embed it, Claude Code, the eMudhra trust probe, Tailscale, Chrome
and macOS, servers, breached platforms, hygiene) and applies each of the nine
fixes only after the word "yes" is typed, announcing every sudo and re-running
the matching check afterwards. The two trust fixes embed no certificate
fingerprints: they fetch the incident page's two lists at run time and refuse
unless each file's sha256 equals the value pinned in the script after a human
review. The checks write nothing, print no secret, and read the Tailscale
daemon's version from the app bundle so a stale Homebrew CLI is flagged as a
second install rather than read as the daemon.

subject: fix(compat): a real file lock on Windows, so concurrent appends keep every record (GRIP#8752) (#8759)
what: Fixed a real file lock on Windows, so concurrent appends keep every record (GRIP#8752) (#8759).
why:
On Windows the _compat shim's flock() did nothing, on the theory that
atomic tempfile+rename keeps files whole. Rename does not protect an
append, so concurrent writers lost records from the signed decision
chain. Measured on Windows 11: six processes appending 300 records to
one chain kept 184, 188 and 184 of them in three runs, and two of those
runs also left a line that does not parse.

subject: feat(tick): the recovery checkpoint act, behind the operator's grant (W4b) (#8822)
what: Added the recovery checkpoint act, behind the operator's grant (W4b) (#8822).
why:
The always-on tick takes its first autonomous act, and only behind every clause
of its gate: a grant for the checkpoint act that verified on this tick, whose
triggers name the incident's kind (a hot or a stuck session), no checkpoint yet
for that incident, and room under the grant's storage cap. The act copies the
session's transcript through its last complete record into a folder the tick
owns, records the offset, the byte count and the SHA-256 of the copy in an
index, and seals the act as an IDR leaf; a seal that fails is recorded in the
index and in the report, never hidden. The act reads the source and never
writes to it, never pauses or signals the session, and never runs on a dry run.
Its own finding travels with the tick's report, so the operator hears of every
checkpoint, every skip for a full cap and every failure. bin/grip-tick-checkpoint
lists the checkpoints and removes one, which is the act's reversal.

subject: fix(windows): the session registry asks psutil whether a session is alive (GRIP#8817) (#8825)
what: Fixed the session registry asks psutil whether a session is alive (GRIP#8817) (#8825).
why:
On Windows, CPython sends os.kill(pid, 0) as a console CTRL_C_EVENT, so it is no
probe. Measured on 2026-10-29 on Windows 11: it answered for the caller's own
children, raised OSError for every live process outside its tree that was tried
(winerror 87 for explorer.exe and the desktop app, 5 for the System process), and
still answered for a child that had exited while its handle was open.
SessionInfo.is_alive maps that OSError to dead. Every registry lock on this machine
holds pid 1 today, so nothing has broken yet. But once the locks hold real PIDs,
which is the next fix, one session would read every other live session as dead and
delete its lock.

subject: fix(windows): the session wizard counts the other live sessions (GRIP#8280) (#8834)
what: Fixed the session wizard counts the other live sessions (GRIP#8280) (#8834).
why:
Every gg++ launch counts the other live sessions so that a second session gets
its own worktree instead of sharing the main checkout. On Windows that count was
blind. Git Bash has no pgrep, so a running session was invisible; and
os.kill(pid, 0) raises OSError there, which the wizard reads as alive, so a launch
that had died still counted for its claim's 600 seconds, while a session older
than that did not count at all.

subject: fix(windows): the stale-worktree reaper runs on Windows (GRIP#8280) (#8837)
what: Fixed the stale-worktree reaper runs on Windows (GRIP#8280) (#8837).
why:
On a concurrent launch the session wizard removes session worktrees whose owner
has ended and that hold nothing to lose. On Windows it never removed any. It
needs the working folder of every live session, read with lsof, which Git Bash
does not have, and it judged a branch lock's owner with os.kill(pid, 0), which
reads every Windows PID as alive. So session worktrees piled up: nine on this
machine by 2026-10-14, later removed by hand.

subject: fix(tick): the keychain holds the signing key's 32-byte seed, because the prompt keeps 128 characters (#8842)
what: Fixed the keychain holds the signing key's 32-byte seed, because the prompt keeps 128 characters (#8842).
why:

why:
On Windows, lib/session_coordinator.py's _is_pid_alive called os.kill(pid, 0).
Windows has no signal 0: CPython sends Ctrl+C to the console process group with
that number instead of checking that a process exists. A branch lock also
records a Git Bash PID, which no Windows call can see. So the check read a live
lock owner as dead, and `cleanup` would remove its lock. With an unlucky PID it
could also send Ctrl+C to a process group on the same console.

subject: fix(windows): session-broadcast judges the control server's PID from Git's ps -W (GRIP#8883, part one) (#8887)
what: Fixed session-broadcast judges the control server's PID from Git's ps -W (GRIP#8883, part one) (#8887).
why:
hooks/session-broadcast.py falls back to scanning for control-server sockets,
and it skips a socket whose server has died. It judged that with
os.kill(pid, 0). Windows has no signal 0: CPython sends Ctrl+C to the console
process group with that number instead of checking that a process exists. The
PID file also holds bash's $! from hooks/session-start.sh or
scripts/grip-pair.sh, a Git Bash PID that no Windows call can see. So a live
server read as dead, and with an unlucky PID the check could send Ctrl+C to a
process group on the same console.

subject: fix(windows): the RSI lock judges its owner's PID without os.kill (GRIP#8883, part two) (#8948)
what: Fixed the RSI lock judges its owner's PID without os.kill (GRIP#8883, part two) (#8948).
why:

and it asked os.kill(pid, 0) whether that process still ran. On Windows that
call does not check anything: CPython sends Ctrl+C to the console process group
with that number. Every /closeout reaches it through check_rsi_lock while a lock
file exists, and acquire_rsi_lock reaches it when an RSI loop starts.

subject: test(mcp-tunnel): press Ctrl-C again when CPython loses the first (GRIP#9045) (#9057)
what: Added tests for press Ctrl-C again when CPython loses the first (GRIP#9045) (#9057).
why:
The ceremony test's Ctrl-C case failed once on CI: the child printed its
prompt, ignored Ctrl-C for 20 seconds and was killed. CPython can explain
that. input() writes its prompt first and only then starts to read. A
SIGINT that arrives in between is recorded by the handler, but nothing
checks that record before the read blocks, so the read waits for more
input. The test sends Ctrl-C the moment the prompt appears, so it can land
in that window. Of the three answers, Ctrl-C is the only one sent as a
signal, and it is the only one that has hung.

subject: test(mcp-tunnel): stop the reaper from writing macOS crash reports (#9062)

subject: fix(black-october): the Windows checker runs no code from the folder it starts in (GRIP#8858) (#8979)
what: Fixed the Windows checker runs no code from the folder it starts in (GRIP#8858) (#8979).
why:
A security fix to the checker merged in GRIP#8967. Each program it ran
started in the folder the script was started from. A Python imports a
certifi.py or a pip package from that folder before its own, so running
check from a folder that holds such files, for example a downloaded
repository, ran them as the user. Measured 2026-11-05 with a planted
certifi.py and pip package that only wrote a marker: the check's reading
said pip 9999.0.0 and certifi 9999.1.1, and both markers were written. A
planted uv.toml naming a mirror also turned 11 of uv's Python download
addresses to that mirror in "uv python list --show-urls".

subject: fix(black-october): two security fixes for the bash checker (GRIP#8971, GRIP#8977) (#9050)
what: Fixed two security fixes for the bash checker (GRIP#8971, GRIP#8977) (#9050).
why:
bin/grip-black-october's `fix npm-tokens` printed a token in full when its
.npmrc line had spaces around the equals sign, because the mask matched only
"_authToken=". npm reads that form as a real token, so the command showed the
very thing it promises to hide. The mask now covers everything after the word
_authToken, which is the rule the Windows twin uses.

what: Fixed route the Python publisher's push through the App gate (GRIP#9013) (#9070).
why:
live_publish in lib/decision_chain_publish.py committed with the machine's
git identity and pushed with a plain `git push`. That bypassed

as the GitHub App or not at all. If the operator's gated `live` step ran on

subject: fix(hooks): read the Stop payload's final message, so a (mine) closer is never missed (#9074)
what: Fixed read the Stop payload's final message, so a (mine) closer is never missed (#9074).
why:
The armed next-step hook is meant to keep a session working when its turn
ends on "RECOMMENDED NEXT STEP (mine)". It read the final message from the
transcript file alone, and that file can lag behind the Stop event. When it
lagged, the hook saw no closer and let the turn end. In the seven days to
2026-11-09, 73 turns on this machine ended on a (mine) closer: the hook
continued 20, and let 53 stop without logging them, because it never saw
them. Each of those 53 sessions stopped on a step it had just called its
own. On one such stop the hook ran 0.4 s after the message and returned

subject: fix(chain): name the exit code in push-failure reasons, with AGORA's follow-up tests (GRIP#9076, GRIP#9077) (#9078)
what: Fixed name the exit code in push-failure reasons, with AGORA's follow-up tests (GRIP#9076, GRIP#9077) (#9078).
why:
_chain_push returned only the last three stderr lines when the gate failed, and
showed the exit code only when stderr was empty. A gate that crashed therefore
read the same as a gate that refused. The reason now always starts with
"chain_push exited N", followed by the stderr tail when there is one.

subject: fix(chain): keep only the stderr lines that say something in a push-failure reason (GRIP#9079) (#9080)
what: Fixed keep only the stderr lines that say something in a push-failure reason (GRIP#9079) (#9080).
why:
_chain_push took the last three lines of the gate's stderr after stripping only
its two ends, so a blank or whitespace-only line inside stderr became an empty
segment and pushed a real line out of the reason. For stderr of "first",
"second", a blank line, a line of spaces, "third" and "fourth", the reason was
"chain_push exited 3:     | third | fourth". It now drops blank lines first and
returns "chain_push exited 3: second | third | fourth".

subject: fix(hooks): the advisory Stop hooks read the payload's copy of the final message (GRIP#9075) (#9082)
what: Fixed the advisory Stop hooks read the payload's copy of the final message (GRIP#9075) (#9082).
why:
The Stop transcript is written separately and can lag behind the Stop event,
so a hook that reads the final message from it alone can act on the previous
message. GRIP#9074 fixed the two hooks whose decisions hang on that message.
